In a short JASA retrospective, Michael Vorländer revisits Leo Beranek and Harvey Sleeper Jr.’s 1946 paper “The design and construction of anechoic sound chambers,” written when such rooms barely existed. Harvard needed free-field conditions for developing acoustic instruments, independent of weather and away from the public. Finding E. H. Bedell’s muslin-and-flannel design unsatisfactory, the authors adopted the porous wedges of Erwin Meyer and colleagues in Berlin, whose chamber had “thousands of acoustic stalactites and stalagmites.”

Their key contribution was optimizing the wedges. They measured nearly 1,000 configurations in an impedance tube 8 in. square and 15 ft long, recording reflected pressure amplitude rather than absorbed energy, for high sensitivity above 99% absorption. An air gap behind the wedges improved low-frequency absorption, and glass-fiber wedges offered the best flow resistance. Two chambers followed, with net working spaces of 29 × 41 × 29 ft and 7 × 11 × 6 ft. Validation checked the inverse distance law: from 70 Hz to 10 kHz, deviations ranged from ±0.3 dB at 4–10 ft to 1.5 dB at 30–40 ft, with instrument accuracy put at ±0.1 dB.

In 1946 the word “anechoic” was so new that the paper footnoted its pronunciation. Yet nearly everything it describes, from wedge design and construction to validation, matches practice today, codified in ISO 3745 (first published 1977) and ISO 26101. Eighty years of measurements, from sound power to HRTFs, have relied on it, and Harvard’s chamber would still rank among the world’s best.

Adapted into Chinese by Fanyu Meng from “All we know about anechoic chambers” by Michael Vorländer, published in The Journal of the Acoustical Society of America 157, R1–R2 (2025). Read the original.
